blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ XXIII
REDUCTIVE GROUPS: UNIQUENESS OF PINNED GROUPSby M. Demazure

The aim of this exposé is the proof of the uniqueness theorem (Theorem 4.1). It was proved by CHEVALLEY in the case of an algebraically closed field; the method of reduction to rank two used here is likewise due to CHEVALLEY (see BIBLE, exp. 23 and 24). Along the way, we obtain an explicit description of reductive groups by generators and relations (3.5).
1. Pinnings

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group (XXII, 1.13). By a pinning of this split group one means the datum of a system of simple roots \(R_0\) of \(R\) and, for each \(\alpha \in R_0\), of a section \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^*\).
In other words, a pinning of the reductive group \(G\) over the non-empty prescheme \(S\) is the datum of:

1. (i)

    a maximal torus \(T\),

  2. (ii)

    an abelian group \(M\) and an isomorphism \(T \simeq D_S(M)\),

  3. (iii)

    a root system \(R\) of \(G\) with respect to \(T\),

  4. (iv)

    a system of simple roots \(R_0\) of \(R\),

  5. (v)

    an \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^*\) for every \(\alpha \in R_0\), that is to say a \[ u_\alpha = \exp_\alpha(X_\alpha) \in U_\alpha^*(S) \quad \text{for all } \alpha \in R_0, \] satisfying condition (D 1) of Exp. XXII, 1.13 (indeed condition (D 2) of loc. cit. is automatically satisfied).
Every split group possesses a pinning; in particular, every reductive group is locally pinnable for the étale topology.

If \(G\) is a pinned \(S\)-group, that is to say a split \(S\)-group equipped with a pinning, it is canonically equipped with the system of positive roots \(R^+\) defined by \(R_0\), with the corresponding Borel group \(B = B_{R^+}\), with the opposite Borel group \(B^- = B_{R^-}\), with the unipotent groups \(U = B_u\), \(U^- = (B^-)_u\), with the open set \(U^- \cdot T \cdot U\), etc... Likewise, for each \(\alpha \in R_0\), one has a canonical isomorphism of vector groups \[ p_\alpha : \mathbb{G}_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_\alpha \] (defined by \(p_\alpha(x) = \exp_\alpha(x X_\alpha) = u_\alpha^x\)), normalised by \(T\) with multiplier \(\alpha\), and whose datum is equivalent to that of \(X_\alpha\) (Exp. XXII, 1.1).

By duality, one deduces from it an \(X_{-\alpha} \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}_{-\alpha})^*\) and an isomorphism \[ p_{-\alpha} : \mathbb{G}_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_{-\alpha} \] which is the contragredient of the preceding one (Exp. XXII, 1.3). We shall set (Exp. XX, 3.1) \[ w_\alpha = w_\alpha(X_\alpha) = p_\alpha(1)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1)\, p_\alpha(1) = p_{-\alpha}(-1)\, p_\alpha(1)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1). \] One then has (loc. cit. 3.1, 3.7) \[ w_\alpha^2 = \alpha^*(-1), \qquad \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) t = s_\alpha(t) = t \cdot \alpha^*(\alpha(t)^{-1}), \] \[ \begin{cases} \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_{-\alpha}(-x) = p_{-\alpha}(x)^{-1}, \\ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\alpha = -X_{-\alpha}, \end{cases} \] \[ \begin{cases} \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\, p_{-\alpha}(x) = p_\alpha(-x) = p_\alpha(x)^{-1}, \\ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{-\alpha} = -X_\alpha. \end{cases} \] We shall use the preceding notations systematically in what follows.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R, R_0, (X_\alpha))\) and \((G', T', M', \ldots)\) two pinned \(S\)-groups. One says that the morphism of split groups (Exp. XXII, 4.2.1) \[ f : G \longrightarrow G' \] is compatible with the pinnings, or defines a morphism of pinned groups, if (notations of loc. cit.) \(u(R_0) = R'_0\) and if, for every \(\alpha \in R_0\), one has \[ f(\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)) = \exp_{u(\alpha)}(X'_{u(\alpha)}), \quad \text{i.e.} \quad f(u_\alpha) = u'_{u(\alpha)}. \]

If one denotes by \(q(\alpha)\) the integer of loc. cit., one thus has \[ f(p_\alpha(x)) = p'_{u(\alpha)}(x^{q(\alpha)}) \quad \text{for } \alpha \in R_0, \] hence also \[ f(p_{-\alpha}(x)) = p'_{-u(\alpha)}(x^{q(\alpha)}), \] \[ f(w_\alpha) = w'_{u(\alpha)}. \] Let us recall (Exp. XXII, 4.2) that one has, for every \(\alpha \in R\) and all \(z \in \mathbb{G}_m(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\): \[ f(\alpha^*(z)) = u(\alpha)^*(z)^{q(\alpha)} = u(\alpha)^*(z^{q(\alpha)}), \] \[ u(\alpha)(f(t)) = \alpha(t)^{q(\alpha)}. \]

Let us call pinned root datum a root datum equipped with a system of simple roots, and \(p\)-morphism of pinned root data a \(p\)-morphism of root data (Exp. XXI, 6.8) taking simple roots to simple roots.

If \(G\) is a pinned \(S\)-group, one denotes by \(\mathcal{R}(G)\) the corresponding pinned root datum (it is the root datum of Exp. XXII, 1.14 equipped with \(R_0\)). Let \(p\) be the integer defined in Exp. XXII, 4.2.2. One then has

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium 1.6

\(G \mapsto \mathcal{R}(G)\) defines a functor from the category of pinned reductive \(S\)-groups into that of pinned root data (with \(p\)-morphisms).
1.7. The pinned groups \(Z_{R_1}\)

Let \(R_1\) be a subset of the system of simple roots \(R_0\) of the pinned group \(G\). Let \(T_{R_1}\) be the maximal torus of \(\bigcap_{\alpha \in R_1} \operatorname{Ker}(\alpha)\); set \[ Z_{R_1} = \underline{\operatorname{Centr}}_G(T_{R_1}). \]

Let us write \(R' = \mathbb{Z} \cdot R_1 \cap R\); it is known (Exp. XXII, 5.10.7) that \(Z_{R_1}\) is a reductive \(S\)-group, with radical \(T_{R_1}\), that \((T, M, R')\) is a splitting of it and \(R_1\) a system of simple roots. It follows that \((Z_{R_1}, T, M, R', R_1, (X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_1})\) is a pinned \(S\)-group. We shall always equip \(Z_{R_1}\) with this pinning. In particular, one will consider the groups \[ Z_\alpha = Z_{\{\alpha\}}, \qquad Z_{\alpha\beta} = Z_{\{\alpha, \beta\}}. \]

One will write \(B_{R_1} = B \cap Z_{R_1}\); it is known (loc. cit.) that this is the canonical Borel group of \(Z_{R_1}\), and that its unipotent part is \(U_{R_1} = U \cap Z_{R_1}\). In particular, one has \[ B_\alpha = T \cdot U_\alpha, \qquad U_\alpha = P_\alpha. \]

One will write \[ U_{\alpha\beta} = U_{\{\alpha,\beta\}} = U \cap Z_{\alpha\beta} = \prod_{\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}} U_\gamma, \] where \(A_{\alpha\beta}\) is the set of positive roots that are linear combinations of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

Let now \(f : G \to G'\) be a morphism of pinned \(S\)-groups. If \(u : R \to R'\) is the corresponding bijection and if \(R_1\) is a subset of \(R_0\), \(u(R_1) = R'_1\) is a subset of \(R'_0\), and it is clear that \(f\) sends \(T_{R_1}\) into \(T'_{R'_1}\), hence \(Z_{R_1}\) into \(Z'_{R'_1}\). The corresponding \(S\)-morphism: \[ f_{R_1} : Z_{R_1} \longrightarrow Z'_{u(R'_1)} \] is compatible with the canonical pinnings; it defines a morphism of pinned root data \[ \mathcal{R}(f_{R_1}) : \mathcal{R}(Z_{R_1}, T, M, \ldots) \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}(Z_{R'_1}, T', M', \ldots) \] and the morphisms \(M' \to M\) underlying \(\mathcal{R}(f)\) and \(\mathcal{R}(f_{R_1})\) coincide.
1.8. Study of the group \(\operatorname{Norm}_G(T)\)

For each pair \((\alpha, \beta)\) of simple roots, let us denote by \(n_{\alpha\beta}\) the order of the element \(s_\alpha s_\beta\) of the Weyl group \(W\). In particular, one has \(n_{\alpha\alpha} = 1\). One therefore has \((w_\alpha w_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}} \in T(S)\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.8.1

For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), one sets \[ t_{\alpha\beta} = (w_\alpha w_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}} \in T(S). \] Moreover, one sets (Exp. XX, 3.1) \[ t_\alpha = t_{\alpha\alpha} = w_\alpha^2 = \alpha^*(-1) \in T(S). \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.8.2

Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-functor in groups taking direct sums of preschemes to products (for example a sheaf for the Zariski topology). Let \[ f_T : T \longrightarrow H \] be a morphism of groups and let \(h_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) be elements of \(H(S)\). For there to exist a morphism of groups (necessarily unique) \[ f_N : \operatorname{Norm}_G(T) \longrightarrow H \] inducing \(f_T\) on \(T\) and such that \(f(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\) for \(\alpha \in R_0\), it is necessary and sufficient that the two following conditions be satisfied:

  1. (i)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\), one has \[ f_T(s_\alpha(t)) = h_\alpha\, f_T(t)\, h_\alpha^{-1} \] for every \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\) (i.e. \(f_T \circ s_\alpha = \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha) \circ f_T\)).

  2. (ii)

    For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), one has \[ f_T(t_{\alpha\beta}) = (h_\alpha h_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}}. \]

Let us indeed equip \((\mathrm{Sch})\) with the topology \(\mathcal{T}\) generated by the pretopology whose covering families are the direct sums; the hypothesis of the statement says that \(H\) is a \(\mathcal{T}\)-sheaf. Let \(L\) be the free group on the generators \((m_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R}\) and \(L_1\) the invariant subgroup generated by the elements \((m_\alpha m_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}}\), \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\). Let \(g : L \to W\) be the morphism defined by \(g(m_\alpha) = s_\alpha\); it is known (Exp. XXI, 5.1) that \(g\) induces an isomorphism \(\bar{g}\) of \(L/L_1\) onto \(W\). Let us make \(L\) operate on \(T\) through \(g\) (or, what amounts to the same, by \(m_\alpha \cdot t = s_\alpha(t)\)). Let \(L_S\) be the constant group defined by \(L\); let us consider the semi-direct product \(T \cdot L_S = N\) for the preceding operation. One has a morphism of \(S\)-groups \[ h : T \cdot L_S = N \longrightarrow \operatorname{Norm}_G(T) \] unique such that \(h(m_\alpha) = w_\alpha\), \(h(t) = t\) for every \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Let \(N_1\) be the invariant subsheaf in groups of \(N\) generated by the \[ t_{\alpha\beta}^{-1} \cdot (m_\alpha m_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}}, \qquad (\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0. \] One obviously has \(N_1 \subset \operatorname{Ker} h\); let us consider the induced morphism \[ h_1 : N/N_1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Norm}_G(T). \]

Let us prove that \(h_1\) is an isomorphism. Since \(h\) induces on \(T\) the canonical immersion, which is a monomorphism, the canonical morphism \[ T \longrightarrow N/N_1 \] is also a monomorphism, hence induces an isomorphism of \(T\) onto \(TN_1/N_1\). For the same reason \(h_1\) induces an isomorphism of \(TN_1/N_1\) onto \(T\); in order to prove that \(h_1\) is an isomorphism, it therefore suffices to check that the corresponding morphism \[ h_2 : N/TN_1 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)/T \] is an isomorphism. Now \(TN_1\) is the invariant sub-\(\mathcal{T}\)-sheaf in groups of \(N\) generated by \(T\) and the \((m_\alpha m_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}}\), that is to say the sub-\(\mathcal{T}\)-sheaf generated by \(T\) and \(L_1\), that is to say \(T \cdot (L_1)_S\). The morphism \(h_2\) is thus identified with the morphism \[ \bar{g} : L_S/(L_1)_S \longrightarrow W_S \] which is an isomorphism by construction.

The proof of 1.8.2 is now easy; the conditions are obviously necessary; let us prove that they are sufficient. Condition (i) shows that there exists a morphism \[ u : N \longrightarrow H \] such that \(u(m_\alpha) = h_\alpha\) for \(\alpha \in R_0\), and \(u|_T = f_T\). Condition (ii) says that \(u\) vanishes on \(N_1\), which yields the result at once.
1.9. Faithfulness of the functor \(\mathcal{R}\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.9.1

The functor \(\mathcal{R}\) of 1.6 is faithful: if \[ f, g : G \rightrightarrows G' \] are two morphisms of pinned groups such that \(\mathcal{R}(f) = \mathcal{R}(g)\), then \(f = g\).
Indeed, \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\), \(U_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) and \(U_{-\alpha}\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\); it therefore suffices to apply:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.9.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned reductive \(S\)-group, \(H\) an \(S\)-presheaf in groups, separated for (fppf). Let \[ f, g : G \rightrightarrows H \] be two morphisms of \(S\)-groups. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(f = g\).

  2. (ii)

    \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\), on each \(U_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\), on each \(U_{-\alpha}\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\).

  3. (iii)

    \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\), on each \(U_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) and \(f(w_\alpha) = g(w_\alpha)\) for each \(\alpha \in R_0\).

Indeed, (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) is trivial, (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) follows at once from the definition of \(w_\alpha\) (1.2). It remains to prove (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). If \(\alpha \in R\), there exists a sequence \(\{\alpha_i\} \subset R_0\) with \(\alpha = s_{\alpha_1} s_{\alpha_2} \cdots s_{\alpha_n}(\alpha_{n+1})\), hence \[ U_\alpha = \operatorname{int}(w_{\alpha_1} \cdots w_{\alpha_n}) U_{\alpha_{n+1}}, \] which proves that \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on each \(U_\alpha\). It follows that \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(\Omega\), hence coincide (Exp. XXII, 4.1.11).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.9.3

If \(G\) is semi-simple, one may, in (ii) and (iii), drop the hypothesis that \(f\) and \(g\) coincide on \(T\). Indeed, \(G\) is generated as an (fppf) sheaf by the \(U_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\) (Exp. XXII, 6.2.2 (a)).

pages.title: 2. Generators and relations for a pinned group

blocks.html: 2. Generators and relations for a pinned group
In this no., we fix a pinned \(S\)-group \(G\). If \(\alpha, \beta \in R_0\), we shall use the notations \(Z_\alpha\), \(Z_{\alpha\beta}\), \(U_{\alpha\beta}\), \(A_{\alpha\beta}\) of 1.7.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(H\) an \(S\)-sheaf in groups for (fppf). Let \[ f_N : \operatorname{Norm}_G(T) \longrightarrow H, \] \[ f_\alpha : U_\alpha \longrightarrow H, \qquad \alpha \in R, \] be morphisms of groups. For there to exist a morphism of groups (necessarily unique) \[ f : G \longrightarrow H \] extending \(f_N\) and the \(f_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R)\), it is necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be satisfied:

  1. (i)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\) and every \(\beta \in R\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(f_N(w_\alpha)) \circ f_\beta = f_{s_\alpha(\beta)} \circ \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha). \]

  2. (ii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\), there exists a morphism of groups \[ F_\alpha : Z_\alpha \longrightarrow H \] extending \(f_\alpha\), \(f_{-\alpha}\) and \(f_N|_{\operatorname{Norm}_{Z_\alpha}(T)}\).

  3. (iii)

    For every pair \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), there exists a morphism of groups \(U_{\alpha\beta} \to H\) inducing \(f_\gamma\) on \(U_\gamma\) for \(\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}\) (i.e. \(U_\gamma \subset U_{\alpha\beta}\)).

Proof. The conditions of the statement are obviously necessary. Let us on the other hand choose a structure of totally ordered group on \(\Gamma_0(R)\) in such a way that the roots \(> 0\) are the elements of \(R^+\) (Exp. XXI, 3.5.6); every product indexed by a subset of \(R\) will be taken relative to this order. Let us denote by \(f_T\) the restriction of \(f_N\) to \(T\) and consider the morphism \[ f : \Omega \longrightarrow H \] defined set-theoretically by \[ f\!\left(\prod_{\alpha \in R^-} y_\alpha \cdot t \cdot \prod_{\alpha \in R^+} x_\alpha\right) = \prod f_\alpha(y_\alpha) \cdot f_T(t) \cdot \prod f_\alpha(x_\alpha). \]

Every morphism satisfying the conditions of the statement must extend \(f\); on the other hand every morphism of groups \(\bar{f} : G \to H\) extending \(f\) also extends \(f_N\): indeed, extending \(f_\alpha\) and \(f_{-\alpha}\), it satisfies \(\bar{f}(w_\alpha) = F_\alpha(w_\alpha) = f_N(w_\alpha)\), and it extends \(f_T\) by hypothesis. By Exp. XXII, 4.1.11 (ii), one is thus reduced to proving:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1.2

The morphism \(f : \Omega \to H\) defined above is "generically multiplicative"; more precisely, for every \(S' \to S\) and all \(x, y \in \Omega(S')\) such that \(xy \in \Omega(S')\), one has \(f(xy) = f(x) f(y)\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.3

If \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S')\), \(S' \to S\), and if \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) with \(\operatorname{int}(n) U_\alpha = U_\beta\), i.e. \(n(\alpha) = \beta\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(f_N(n)) \circ f_\alpha = f_\beta \circ \operatorname{int}(n). \]

Indeed, it suffices to check the formula for a system of generators of the sheaf \(\operatorname{Norm}_G(T)\); it is true for each \(w_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\) (by (i)), so it suffices to do it for \(n \in T(S')\). This is trivial by (ii) if \(\alpha\) is simple; otherwise, one takes a \(w \in W\) such that \(w^{-1}(\alpha) \in R_0\); writing \(w\) as a product of fundamental symmetries, one is reduced to proving that if the formula is true for \(\alpha\) and for every \(n\), it is also true for \(w_{\alpha_0}(\alpha)\) and \(t \in T(S')\), where \(\alpha_0 \in R_0\). Now, by (i), one has: \[ \operatorname{int}(f_N(t)) \circ f_{w_{\alpha_0}(\alpha)} = \operatorname{int}(f_N(t w_{\alpha_0})) \circ f_\alpha \circ \operatorname{int}(w_{\alpha_0}^{-1}) \] \[ = f_{w_{\alpha_0}(\alpha)} \circ \operatorname{int}(t w_{\alpha_0}) \circ \operatorname{int}(w_{\alpha_0}^{-1}). \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.4

The restriction of \(f\) to \(U\) (resp. \(U^-\)) is a morphism of groups. In particular, this restriction is independent of the order chosen on the roots.

It suffices to give the proof for \(U\). By virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.5.8, it suffices to check that for every pair \(\alpha < \beta\) of positive roots one has, for all \(x_\alpha \in U_\alpha(S')\), \(x_\beta \in U_\beta(S')\), \(S' \to S\), \[ f_\beta(x_\beta)\, f_\alpha(x_\alpha)\, f_\beta(x_\beta^{-1}) = f(x_\beta\, x_\alpha\, x_\beta^{-1}). \] By virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.5.2 there exist \(x_\gamma \in U_\gamma(S')\) \((\gamma = i\alpha + j\beta \in R,\, i, j > 0)\) with \[ x_\beta\, x_\alpha\, x_\beta^{-1} = \prod_\gamma x_\gamma, \] and one must therefore check the relation \[ f_\beta(x_\beta)\, f_\alpha(x_\alpha)\, f_\beta(x_\beta^{-1}) = \prod_{\substack{\gamma = i\alpha + j\beta \\ i, j > 0}} f_\gamma(x_\gamma). \] By Exp. XXI, 3.5.4, there exists a \(w \in W\) such that \(w(\alpha) = \alpha_0 \in R_0\), \(w(\beta) \in A_{\alpha_0 \beta_0}\) (notations of 1.7), where \(\beta_0 \in R_0\). Lifting \(w\) to an \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) (by Exp. XXII, 3.8), it suffices to check the preceding relation after conjugation by \(f_N(n)\). By 2.1.3, one is thus reduced to the case where \(\alpha, \beta \in A_{\alpha_0 \beta_0}\), a case in which one concludes by condition (iii).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.5

Let \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) be such that \(\operatorname{int}(n) U = U^-\) (i.e. such that \(n\) is the symmetry of the Weyl group (Exp. XXI, 3.6.14)). For every \(u \in U(S')\), \(S' \to S\) (resp. \(u \in U^-(S')\), \(S' \to S\)), one has \[ f(n u n^{-1}) = f_N(n)\, f(u)\, f_N(n^{-1}). \]
Immediate by 2.1.3 and 2.1.4.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.6

Let \(u \in B(S')\), \(v \in B^-(S')\), \(g \in \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Then \[ f(v g u) = f(v)\, f(g)\, f(u). \]

Indeed, let us set \(v = v_1 t_1\), \(g = v_2 t_2 u_2\), \(u = t_3 u_3\), with \(v_i \in U^-(S')\), \(t_i \in T(S')\), \(u_i \in U(S')\). One has \[ f(v)\, f(g)\, f(u) = f(v_1)\, f_T(t_1)\, f(v_2)\, f_T(t_2)\, f(u_2)\, f_T(t_3)\, f(u_3), \] on the one hand, and \[ f(v g u) = f(v_1 t_1 v_2 t_1^{-1} \cdot t_1 t_2 t_3 \cdot t_3^{-1} u_2 t_3 \cdot u_3) \] \[ = f(v_1 \cdot t_1 v_2 t_1^{-1})\, f_T(t_1 t_2 t_3)\, f(t_3^{-1} u_2 t_3 \cdot u_3). \] Using 2.1.4 to decompose the two outer terms of this last expression, one obtains \[ f(v g u) = f(v_1)\, f(t_1 v_2 t_1^{-1})\, f_T(t_1 t_2 t_3)\, f(t_3^{-1} u_2 t_3)\, f(u_3). \] One is then reduced to the obvious formulas \[ f(t_1 v_2 t_1^{-1}) = f_T(t_1)\, f(v_2)\, f_T(t_1)^{-1}, \] \[ f(t_3^{-1} u_2 t_3) = f_T(t_3)^{-1}\, f(u_2)\, f_T(t_3), \] which follow from the definition of \(f\) and from 2.1.3.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.7

Let \(\alpha \in R_0\) and \(g \in \Omega(S') \cap \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)^{-1} \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Then \[ f(w_\alpha\, g\, w_\alpha^{-1}) = f_N(w_\alpha)\, f(g)\, f_N(w_\alpha)^{-1}. \]

Indeed, let \(g \in \Omega(S')\), \(S' \to S\). Let us write, by Exp. XXII, 5.6.8 \[ g = a\, x_{-\alpha}\, t\, x_\alpha\, b, \] with \(a \in \widehat{U}^-_\alpha(S')\), \(x_{-\alpha} \in U_{-\alpha}(S')\), \(t \in T(S')\), \(x_\alpha \in U_\alpha(S')\), \(b \in \widehat{U}_\alpha(S')\). By 2.1.3, 2.1.4 and the fact that \(s_\alpha\) permutes the positive roots \(\neq \alpha\) (cf. Exp. XXI, 3.3.2), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) a \in \widehat{U}^-_\alpha(S'), \qquad \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) b \in \widehat{U}_\alpha(S') \] and the formula to be proved is true for \(g = a\) or \(g = b\). By 2.1.6, one is thus reduced to proving the assertion sought when \(g = x_{-\alpha}\, t\, x_\alpha \in Z_\alpha(S')\). But then "everything takes place in \(Z_\alpha\)" and one concludes by condition (ii) of 2.1.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.1.8

Let \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\). For every \(S' \to S\) and every \(g \in \Omega(S')\) such that \(\operatorname{int}(n) g \in \Omega(S')\), one has \[ f(n g n^{-1}) = f_N(n)\, f(g)\, f_N(n)^{-1}. \]

This is trivial if \(n \in T(S)\) (by 2.1.3). The two sides of the preceding formula define morphisms from \(\Omega \cap \operatorname{int}(n)^{-1} \Omega\) into \(H\); in order to check that they coincide, it suffices to check that there exists an open set \(V_n\) of \(\Omega\), containing the unit section, such that \(\operatorname{int}(n) V_n \subset \Omega\), and that \(f \circ \operatorname{int}(n)\) and \(\operatorname{int}(f_N(n)) \circ f\) coincide on \(V_n\). By virtue of the structure of \(\operatorname{Norm}_G(T)\), it suffices to prove that if the preceding assertion is true for an \(n' \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) and if \(\alpha \in R_0\), it is true for \(n = n' w_\alpha\). Let us set \[ V_n = \Omega \cap \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)^{-1} V_{n'}. \] One has \(\operatorname{int}(n) V_n \subset \operatorname{int}(n') V_{n'} \subset \Omega\). If \(g \in V_n(S')\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(n) g = \operatorname{int}(n') \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) g. \] Now \(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) g \in V_{n'}(S')\), hence by hypothesis \[ f(\operatorname{int}(n') \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) g) = \operatorname{int}(f_N(n'))\, f(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) g)\ ; \] since \(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) g \in \Omega(S')\), one may apply 2.1.7, which gives \[ f(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) g) = \operatorname{int}(f_N(w_\alpha))\, f(g), \] and one concludes at once.

Let us now prove 2.1.2. Let \(x, x' \in \Omega(S')\); let us write as usual \[ x = v t u, \qquad x' = v' t' u', \] whence \[ x x' = v t (u v') t' u'. \] By 2.1.6 and the relation \(U^-(S')\, \Omega(S')\, U(S') = \Omega(S')\), one is reduced to proving that if \(u v' \in \Omega(S')\), one has \(f(u v') = f(u)\, f(v')\). Let \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S')\) be as in 2.1.5 (ii). One has \[ f(u) = f_N(n)^{-1}\, f(n u n^{-1})\, f_N(n), \] \[ f(v') = f_N(n)^{-1}\, f(n v' n^{-1})\, f_N(n), \] by loc. cit., whence \[ f(u)\, f(v') = f_N(n)^{-1}\, f(n u n^{-1})\, f(n v' n^{-1})\, f_N(n). \] But \(n u n^{-1} \in U^-(S')\), \(n v' n^{-1} \in U(S')\), so that \[ f(n u n^{-1})\, f(n v' n^{-1}) = f((n u n^{-1})(n v' n^{-1})) = f(n u v' n^{-1}), \] which gives \[ f(u)\, f(v') = f_N(n)^{-1}\, f(n u v' n^{-1})\, f_N(n). \] If \(u v' \in \Omega(S')\), one may apply 2.1.8 and we are done.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.2

Instead of giving oneself \(f_N\), one may give oneself a morphism of groups \(f_T : T \to H\) and sections \(h_\alpha \in H(S)\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) satisfying the conditions of 1.8.2. Condition (ii) of the theorem must then be replaced by

(ii') There exists a morphism of groups \(F_\alpha : Z_\alpha \to H\) which extends \[ f_\alpha, \; f_{-\alpha}, \; f_T \quad \text{and satisfies } F_\alpha(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha. \]
We shall now give the preceding theorem a more explicit form. Let us keep the preceding notations.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group. Let \(H\) be an \(S\)-sheaf in groups for (fppf), let \[ f_T : T \longrightarrow H, \] \[ f_\alpha : U_\alpha \longrightarrow H, \qquad \alpha \in R_0 \] be morphisms of groups and let \[ h_\alpha \in H(S), \qquad (\alpha \in R_0), \] be sections of \(H\). For there to exist a morphism of groups \[ f : G \longrightarrow H \] (necessarily unique) inducing \(f_T\) and the \(f_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) and satisfying \(f(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\) for every \(\alpha \in R_0\), it is necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be satisfied:

  1. (i)

    For every \(S' \to S\), every \(t \in T(S')\), every \(\alpha \in R_0\) and every \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), one has \[ (1) \qquad f_T(t)\, f_\alpha(x)\, f_T(t)^{-1} = f_\alpha(\operatorname{int}(t) x). \]

  2. (ii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\), every \(S' \to S\), every \(t \in T(S')\), one has \[ (2) \qquad h_\alpha\, f_T(t)\, h_\alpha^{-1} = f_T(s_\alpha(t)) = f_T(t \cdot \alpha^*(\alpha(t)^{-1})). \]

  3. (iii)

    For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), one has \[ (3) \qquad (h_\alpha h_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}} = f_T(t_{\alpha\beta}). \]

  4. (iv)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\), one has (recall that one writes \(u_\alpha = \exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)\)) \[ (4) \qquad (h_\alpha\, f_\alpha(u_\alpha))^3 = e. \]

  5. (v)

    For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), \(\alpha \neq \beta\), there exists a morphism of groups \[ f_{\alpha\beta} : U_{\alpha\beta} \longrightarrow H \] satisfying the two following conditions:

    a) One has \[ (5) \qquad f_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_\alpha} = f_\alpha, \qquad f_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_\beta} = f_\beta, \]

    b) For every \(\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}\), \(\gamma \neq \alpha\) (resp. \(\gamma \neq \beta\)), and every \(x \in U_\gamma(S')\), \(S' \to S\), one has \[ (6) \qquad \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha)\, f_{\alpha\beta}(x) = f_{\alpha\beta}(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha) x), \] \[ (\text{resp.} \quad \operatorname{int}(h_\beta)\, f_{\alpha\beta}(x) = f_{\alpha\beta}(\operatorname{int}(w_\beta) x)). \]
Proof. Uniqueness is clear by 1.9.2. Let us prove existence.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.1

There exists a morphism of groups \[ f_N : \operatorname{Norm}_G(T) \longrightarrow H \] extending \(f_T\) and satisfying \(f_N(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\).
This is indeed what 1.8.2 asserts, taking into account conditions (2) and (3).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.2

There exists a morphism of groups \[ F_\alpha : Z_\alpha \longrightarrow H, \qquad \alpha \in R_0, \] extending \(f_T\), \(f_\alpha\) and satisfying \(F_\alpha(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\), hence extending \(f_N|_{\operatorname{Norm}_{Z_\alpha}(T)}\).
This is clear by Exp. XX, 6.2 and conditions (1), (3) and (4).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.3

For every \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), \(\alpha \neq \beta\), every \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_{Z_{\alpha\beta}}(T)(S)\) such that \(n(\alpha) = \alpha\) (resp. \(n(\alpha) = \beta\)), i.e. \(\operatorname{int}(n) U_\alpha = U_\alpha\) (resp. \(\operatorname{int}(n) U_\alpha = U_\beta\)), every \(S' \to S\) and every \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(f_N(n))\, f_\alpha(x) = f_\alpha(\operatorname{int}(n) x) \] \[ (\text{resp.} \quad \operatorname{int}(f_N(n))\, f_\alpha(x) = f_\beta(\operatorname{int}(n) x)). \]

Indeed, there exist a \(t \in T(S)\) and a sequence \(\{\alpha_i\} \subset \{\alpha, \beta\}\) such that \(n = t w_{\alpha_k} \cdots w_{\alpha_1}\). The condition is satisfied for \(n = t\) by condition (1). One may therefore assume \(n = w_{\alpha_k} \cdots w_{\alpha_1}\). Let us give the proof by induction on \(k\), i.e. let us assume the assertion proved for every \(n\) which can be written as a product of fewer than \(k - 1\) fundamental symmetries (and satisfies the hypotheses of the lemma). Let us consider the roots \[ \gamma_i = s_{\alpha_i} \cdots s_{\alpha_1}(\alpha). \] If all the \(\gamma_i\) are positive, i.e. \(\in A_{\alpha\beta}\), one may apply condition (v) of 2.3; taking the notations of 2.3 (v), one concludes at once by induction that \[ \operatorname{int}(f_N(w_{\alpha_i} \cdots w_{\alpha_1}))\, f_\alpha(x) = f_{\alpha\beta}(\operatorname{int}(w_{\alpha_i} \cdots w_{\alpha_1}) x), \] that is, for \(i = k\), the property sought. If the \(\gamma_i\) are not all positive, there exists a \(j < k\) with \[ \gamma_j \in R^+, \qquad \gamma_{j+1} \notin R^+. \] Since \(\gamma_{j+1} = s_{\alpha_j}(\gamma_j)\), it follows at once that \(\gamma_j = \alpha_j\), by Exp. XXI, 3.3.2, hence that \(\gamma_j\) is \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), and one may decompose \(n\) into \[ n = n' \cdot n'', \] \[ n' = w_{\alpha_k} \cdots w_{\alpha_{j+1}}, \] \[ n'' = w_{\alpha_j} \cdots w_{\alpha_1}, \] \(n'\) and \(n''\) satisfying the hypotheses of the lemma and being products of fewer than \(k - 1\) symmetries, hence satisfying, by the induction hypothesis, the conclusion of the lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.4

Let \(\alpha \in R\). If \(n, n' \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) and \(\beta, \beta' \in R_0\) satisfy \(n(\alpha) = \beta\) and \(n'(\alpha) = \beta'\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(f_T(n))^{-1}\, f_\beta(n\, x\, n^{-1}) = \operatorname{int}(f_T(n'))^{-1}\, f_{\beta'}(n'\, x\, n'^{-1}), \] for every \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

It suffices to check that if \(n(\alpha) = \beta\), \(\alpha, \beta \in R_0\), then \(\operatorname{int}(f_T(n)) \circ f_\alpha = f_\beta \circ \operatorname{int}(n)\). Now by Tits' lemma (Exp. XXI, 5.1), there exist a sequence of simple roots \(\alpha_0 = \alpha, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_m = \beta\), and a sequence of elements \(w_i \in W\), \(i = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1\), with \[ n = w_{m-1} \cdots w_0, \] \[ w_i(\alpha_i) = \alpha_{i+1}, \qquad i = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1, \] the following condition being moreover satisfied: for every \(i = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1\), there exists a simple root \(\beta_i\) such that \[ w_i \in W_{\alpha_i \beta_i}, \qquad \alpha_{i+1} = \alpha_i \quad \text{or} \quad \beta_i. \] One is then reduced, by induction, to the case treated in the preceding lemma.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.3.5

There exists a family \(f'_\gamma\), \(\gamma \in R\), of morphisms of groups \(f'_\gamma : U_\gamma \to H\) satisfying

  1. (i)

    For \(\alpha \in R_0\), one has \(f'_\alpha = f_\alpha\) and \(f'_{-\alpha} = F_\alpha|_{U_{-\alpha}}\) where \(F_\alpha\) is defined in 2.3.2.

  2. (ii)

    For \(\alpha, \beta \in R_0\) and \(\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}\), one has \(f'_\gamma = f_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_\gamma}\).

  3. (iii)

    For every \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) and \(\alpha, \beta \in R\) such that \(n(\alpha) = \beta\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(f_N(n))\, f'_\alpha(x) = f'_\beta(\operatorname{int}(n) x) \] for every \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

For every root \(\alpha \in R\), there exists an \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) such that \(n(\alpha) \in R_0\). We then define \(f'_\alpha(x)\) to be the expression of 2.3.4. The latter is independent of the choice of \(n\), and \(f'_\alpha\) is indeed a group morphism. Property (iii) holds by construction. The first assertion of (i) is clear (take \(n = e\)), and so is the second (take \(n = w_\alpha\) and apply 2.3.2); if \(\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}\), \((\alpha, \beta \in R_0)\), there exists \(n \in \operatorname{Norm}_{Z_{\alpha\beta}}(T)(S)\) such that \(n(\gamma) = \alpha\) or \(\beta\); one then applies (iii) together with conditions (5) and (6), and (ii) is proved.
Let us now prove the theorem, by showing that the conditions of 2.1 are satisfied for the morphisms \(f_N\) and \(f'_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\).
2.1 (i) follows from 2.3.5 (iii),
2.1 (ii) follows from 2.3.5 (i) and 2.3.2,
2.1 (iii) follows from 2.3.5 (ii) and from the fact that \(f_{\alpha\beta}\) is a group morphism.
An obvious corollary is the following:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group of semi-simple rank \(\geqslant 1\), \(H\) an (fppf) \(S\)-sheaf of groups. For each \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), let \[ F_{\alpha\beta} : Z_{\alpha\beta} \longrightarrow H \] be a group morphism. In order for there to exist a group morphism \[ f : G \longrightarrow H \] inducing the \(F_{\alpha\beta}\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\) one have \[ F_{\alpha\beta}|_{Z_\alpha} = F_{\alpha\alpha}. \]

The condition is obviously necessary. Suppose it is satisfied. Set \(f_T = F_{\alpha\alpha}|_T\) (which does not depend on \(\alpha\), since \(F_{\alpha\alpha}|_T = F_{\alpha\beta}|_T = F_{\beta\beta}|_T\)). Set \[ p_\alpha = F_{\alpha\alpha}|_{U_\alpha}, \qquad h_\alpha = F_{\alpha\alpha}(w_\alpha), \qquad f_{\alpha\beta} = F_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_{\alpha\beta}}. \] The conditions of 2.3 are obviously satisfied: (1), (2), (4) "are verified" in \(Z_\alpha\), and (3), (5) and (6) in \(Z_{\alpha\beta}\). There therefore exists a morphism \(f : G \to H\) extending \(f_T\) and the \(f_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\), and satisfying \(f(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\); it coincides with \(F_{\alpha\beta}\) on generators of \(Z_{\alpha\beta}\), hence satisfies \(f|_{Z_{\alpha\beta}} = F_{\alpha\beta}\).
We also have the following technical corollary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two pinned \(S\)-groups of semi-simple rank \(2\), \(q\) an integer \(> 0\) such that \(x \mapsto x^q\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathbb{G}_{a, S}\), and \(h : \mathcal{R}(G') \to \mathcal{R}(G)\) a \(q\)-morphism of pinned root data. For each \(\alpha \in R^+\) choose an \(X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^*\) and an \(X'_{u(\alpha)} \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}'_{u(\alpha)})^*\) (extending the canonical choices for \(\alpha \in R_0\)). Suppose the following conditions are satisfied:

  1. (i)

    If \(R_0 = \{\alpha, \beta\}\), one has \(D_S(h)(t_{\alpha\beta}) = t'_{u(\alpha) u(\beta)}\).

  2. (ii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\) and every \(\beta \in R^+\), \(\beta \neq \alpha\) (whence \(s_\alpha(\beta) \in R^+\)), if \(z \in \mathbb{G}_m(S)\) is defined by \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = z X_{s_\alpha(\beta)}, \] then one also has \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{u(\alpha)}) X'_{u(\beta)} = z^{q(\beta)} X'_{u(s_\alpha(\beta))}. \]

  3. (iii)

    There exists a group morphism \(f : U \to U'\) such that for every \(\alpha \in R^+\) one has, for every \(x \in \mathbb{G}_a(S')\), \(S' \to S\). \[ f(\exp(x X_\alpha)) = \exp(x^{q(\alpha)} X'_{u(\alpha)}). \]

Then there exists a morphism of pinned groups \(G \xrightarrow{g} G'\) such that \(\mathcal{R}(g) = h\).

Indeed, one defines \(f_\alpha : U_\alpha \to G'\) by \[ f_\alpha(\exp(x X_\alpha)) = \exp(x^{q(\alpha)} X'_{u(\alpha)})\ ; \] one sets \(f_T = D_S(h)\), \(h_\alpha = w'_{u(\alpha)}\). The conditions of 2.3 are satisfied (note that \(q(s_\alpha(\beta)) = q(\beta)\) (Exp. XXI, 6.8.4) and that one always has \(D_S(h)(t_\alpha) = t'_{u(\alpha)}\)), and one concludes at once.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 2.6

Condition (v) of 2.3 can be made more precise as follows. One must first check:

(a) For every word in \(w_\alpha\) and \(w_\beta\) such that the corresponding word carries \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) into \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\), the corresponding relation of type 2.3.3 holds. In fact the proof of 2.3.3 shows that it suffices to check this for those words in \(w_\alpha\) and \(w_\beta\) that are minimal (in the sense that no non-trivial initial subword satisfies the imposed conditions).

If condition (a) holds, one may now define, for each \(\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}\), an \(f_\gamma : U_\gamma \to H\) as in 2.3.5; one must then write:

(b) The morphism \[ U_{\alpha\beta} = \prod_{\gamma \in A_{\alpha\beta}} U_\gamma \longrightarrow H \] defined by the \(f_\gamma\) is a group morphism. By Exp. XXII, 5.5.8, (b) is implied by:

(b') The preceding morphism respects the commutation relations between \(U_\gamma\) and \(U_\delta\) for \(\gamma, \delta \in A_{\alpha\beta}\), \(\gamma > \delta\) (i.e. the relations in \(C_{i,j,\gamma,\delta}\) of Exp. XXII, 5.5.2).

It is clear that, conversely, the set of conditions (a) and (b') is equivalent to (v).

One can even reduce the preceding conditions to conditions bearing only on the elements \(h_\alpha\), \(h_\beta\), \(f_\alpha(u_\alpha)\), \(f_\beta(u_\beta)\) of \(H\). A condition of type (a) will read, for example, if \(s_\alpha s_\beta s_\alpha(\beta) = \alpha\): \[ (1) \qquad \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha h_\beta h_\alpha)\, f_\beta(x) = f_\alpha(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha) x)\ ; \] for every \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), \(S' \to S\). In particular, for \(x = u_\beta\), one has \(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha) u_\beta = u_\alpha^z\) for a certain section \(z\) of \(\mathbb{G}_m(S)\), and the preceding relation will give \[ (1') \qquad \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha h_\beta h_\alpha)\, f_\beta(u_\beta) = f_\alpha(u_\alpha)^z. \] Let us show that, conversely, taking into account conditions (i) to (iv) of 2.3, (1') implies (1). If \(t \in T(S')\), \(S' \to S\), let us make \(\operatorname{int}(t)\) act on (1'); taking conditions (i) and (ii) into account, one obtains (1) for \(x = \operatorname{int}(t) u_\beta = u_\beta^{\beta(t)}\). It now suffices to note that \(\beta : T \to \mathbb{G}_{m, S}\) is faithfully flat, so that condition (1) is certainly true for \(x \in U_\alpha(S')^*\), \(S' \to S\). Since it is additive in \(x\), and since every section of \(U_\alpha\) can be written locally as a sum of two sections of \(U_\alpha^*\), we do conclude that (1') + (i) + (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (1).

One argues in the same way with the conditions of type (b). One must then use the fact that if \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\) are two distinct positive roots (and hence linearly independent over \(\mathbb{Q}\)), the morphism \(T \to \mathbb{G}_{m, S}^2\) with components \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma'\) is faithfully flat. We leave the details of this transposition to the reader.
3. Groups of semi-simple rank 2
3.1. Generalities

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) two roots of \(G\), with \(\alpha + \beta \neq 0\).

  1. (i)

    If \(\alpha + \beta \notin R\), one has \[ \exp(X_\alpha)\, \exp(X_\beta) = \exp(X_\beta)\, \exp(X_\alpha) \] for all \(X_\alpha \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\alpha)(S')\), \(X_\beta \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\beta)(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

  2. (ii)

    If \(\alpha + \beta\) and \(\alpha - \beta\) are not roots, one has \[ w_\alpha(z_\alpha)\, \exp(X_\beta)\, w_\alpha(z_\alpha)^{-1} = \exp(X_\beta) \] for all \(X_\beta \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\beta)(S')\), \(z_\alpha \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^*(S')\), \(S' \to S\), and \[ w_\alpha(z_\alpha)\, w_\beta(z_\beta) = w_\beta(z_\beta)\, w_\alpha(z_\alpha) \] for all \(z_\alpha \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^*(S')\) and \(z_\beta \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\beta)^*(S')\), \(S' \to S\).

  3. (iii)

    Let \(X_\alpha \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^*(S')\), \(X_\beta \in W(\mathfrak{g}_\beta)^*(S')\), and \(w \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S')\) be such that \(w(\alpha) = \beta\); define \(z \in \mathbb{G}_m(S')\) by \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w) X_\alpha = z X_\beta. \] Then \[ \operatorname{int}(w)\, \exp(x X_\alpha) = \exp(x z X_\beta), \] \[ \operatorname{int}(w)\, \exp(y X_\alpha^{-1}) = \exp(y z^{-1} X_\beta^{-1}), \] \[ \operatorname{int}(w)\, w_\alpha(X_\alpha) = \beta^*(z)\, w_\beta(X_\beta). \] In particular, if \(z = \pm 1\), one has \[ \operatorname{int}(w)\, w_\alpha(X_\alpha) = w_\beta(X_\beta)^z. \]

  4. (iv)

    If one sets \(t_\alpha = \alpha^*(-1)\), \(t_\beta = \beta^*(-1)\), one has \[ s_\alpha(t_\beta) = t_\beta\, t_\alpha^{(\beta^*, \alpha)}, \qquad \beta(t_\alpha) = (-1)^{(\alpha^*, \beta)}. \]

Proof. (i) follows at once from Exp. XXII, 5.5.2, (ii) from Exp. XX, 3.1 and from (i) applied to \((\beta, \alpha)\), \((\beta, -\alpha)\), \((-\beta, \alpha)\), \((-\beta, -\alpha)\), and (iii) is evident from the definitions; for the last assertion of (iii), note that \(\beta^*(-1) = w_\beta(X_\beta)^{-2}\). Finally, (iv) is trivial.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1.2 (Groups of type \(A_1 \times A_1\))

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(A_1 + A_1\); let us write \(R_0 = R^+ = \{\alpha, \beta\}\).

  1. (i)

    One has \[ t_{\alpha\beta} = (w_\alpha w_\beta)^2 = t_\alpha t_\beta = (w_\beta w_\alpha)^2 = t_{\beta\alpha}. \]

  2. (ii)

    One has \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = X_\beta, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_\alpha. \]

  3. (iii)

    \(U_\alpha\) and \(U_\beta\) commute (i.e. \(U\) is commutative).

Indeed, by assertion (ii) of the lemma, one has \[ w_\alpha w_\beta = w_\beta w_\alpha, \] whence \((w_\alpha w_\beta)^2 = w_\alpha^2 w_\beta^2 = t_\alpha t_\beta\), which is (i). By assertion (ii) of the lemma one likewise has (ii); finally (iii) is assertion (i) of the lemma.

Let us make condition (v) of 2.3 explicit here. Using the method set out in 2.6, one obtains the following two groups of conditions, on setting \(v_\alpha = f_\alpha(u_\alpha)\), for \(\alpha \in R_0\): \[ (A) \begin{cases} h_\alpha\, v_\beta\, h_\alpha^{-1} = v_\beta \\ h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1} = v_\alpha \end{cases} \qquad (B)\; v_\alpha\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_\alpha. \]
3.2. Groups of type \(A_2\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(A_2\); let us write \(R_0 = \{\alpha, \beta\}\), \(R^+ = \{\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta\}\).

  1. (i)

    One has \[ t_{\alpha\beta} = (w_\alpha w_\beta)^3 = e = (w_\beta w_\alpha)^3 = t_{\beta\alpha}. \]

  2. (ii)

    Set \(\operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}\). Then \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = -X_{\alpha+\beta}, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = X_\beta, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = -X_\alpha. \]

  3. (iii)

    Set \(p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{\alpha+\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\beta)\, p_\alpha(x)\). One has: \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy). \]
One has \((\beta^*, \alpha) = (\alpha^*, \beta) = -1\), whence \(\alpha(t_\beta) = \beta(t_\alpha) = -1\).

Set \(\operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}\); one has at once \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = \alpha(t_\beta) X_\alpha = -X_\alpha. \] Set \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = z X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad z \in \mathbb{G}_m(S), \] whence \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = \beta(t_\alpha) z^{-1} X_\beta = -z^{-1} X_\beta. \] We know (Exp. XXII, 5.5.2) that there exists a unique section \(A \in \mathbb{G}_a(S)\) with \[ (+) \qquad p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(A x y). \] In order to prove (ii) and (iii), it is therefore a matter of showing that \(A = -z = 1\).

Let us make \(\operatorname{int}(w_\beta)\) act on the preceding formula \((+)\); one obtains: \[ (++) \qquad p_{-\beta}(-y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-y)\, p_\alpha(-A x y). \]

By the definition of \(p_{\alpha+\beta}\), one has \[ w_\beta\, p_\alpha(x)\, w_\beta^{-1} = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x), \] which reads \[ p_\beta(1)\, p_{-\beta}(-1)\, p_\beta(1)\, p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(-1)\, p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_\beta(-1) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x). \] Since \(p_\beta\) and \(p_{\alpha+\beta}\) commute, \(\alpha + 2\beta\) not being a root, this may also be written \[ p_\beta(1)\, p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(-1) = p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-1). \] Now using \((+)\) on the left-hand side and \((++)\) on the right, one obtains: \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_\beta(-1) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{-\beta}(-1), \] which, \(\alpha + 2\beta\) and \(\alpha - \beta\) not being roots, reads \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_\alpha(Ax). \] Since \(2\alpha + \beta\) is not a root, this gives \(A = 1\).

Let us now make \(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\) act on formula \((+)\); using the fact that \(A = 1\), one finds \[ (+++) \qquad p_{\alpha+\beta}(zy)\, p_{-\alpha}(-x) = p_{-\alpha}(-x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(zy)\, p_\beta(-z^{-1} xy). \]

Let us now write, as before, \[ w_\alpha\, p_\beta(y)\, w_\alpha^{-1} = p_{\alpha+\beta}(zy), \] that is \[ p_\alpha(1)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(-1) = p_{-\alpha}(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(zy)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1). \] Now using \((+)\) and \((+++)\), this may also be written \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-y) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(zy)\, p_\beta(-z^{-1} y), \] and hence gives \(z = -1\).

We have thus proved (ii) and (iii); let us prove (i). One has \[ w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha = w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha^{-1} w_\alpha^2 = w_{\alpha+\beta}^{-1}\, t_\alpha, \] whence \[ w_\beta w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha w_\beta = w_\beta w_{\alpha+\beta}^{-1}\, t_\alpha\, w_\beta = w_\beta w_{\alpha+\beta} w_\beta^{-1} \cdot s_\beta(t_\alpha) \cdot t_\beta \] \[ = w_\alpha \cdot t_\alpha t_\beta \cdot t_\beta = w_\alpha t_\alpha = w_\alpha^{-1}, \] which gives \[ (w_\alpha w_\beta)^3 = (w_\beta w_\alpha)^3 = e, \] and this completes the proof.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.2.8

Condition (v) of 2.3 translates here into the following (writing \(v_\alpha = f_\alpha(u_\alpha)\)): \[ (A)\; h_\alpha\, v_\beta^{-1}\, h_\alpha^{-1} = h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1} \qquad (B) \begin{cases} v_\beta\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_\beta \cdot h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1}, \\ v_\beta \cdot h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1} = h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1} \cdot v_\beta, \\ v_\alpha \cdot h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1} = h_\beta\, v_\alpha\, h_\beta^{-1} \cdot v_\alpha. \end{cases} \] On setting \(v_{\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\beta) v_\alpha\), the last three conditions may also be written \[ (B) \begin{cases} v_\beta\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_\beta\, v_{\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_\alpha\, v_{\alpha+\beta} = v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_\alpha, \\ v_\beta\, v_{\alpha+\beta} = v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_\beta. \end{cases} \]
3.3. Groups of type \(B_2\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.3.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(B_2\); let us write \(R_0 = \{\alpha, \beta\}\), \(R^+ = \{\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta\}\).

  1. (i)

    One has \[ t_{\alpha\beta} = (w_\alpha w_\beta)^4 = t_\alpha = (w_\beta w_\alpha)^4 = t_{\beta\alpha}. \]

  2. (ii)

    If one sets \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \] one has: \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = -X_{\alpha+\beta}, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_\beta, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = -X_\alpha, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}. \]

  3. (iii)

    Set \(p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{\alpha+\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\beta)\, p_\alpha(x)\), \[ p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{2\alpha+\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\, p_\beta(x). \] Then: \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y), \] \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(2xy). \]

One has \((\beta^*, \alpha) = -1\), \((\alpha^*, \beta) = -2\), whence \(\alpha(t_\beta) = -1\), \(\beta(t_\alpha) = 1\). Let us note in passing that \(\beta(t_\alpha) = \alpha(t_\alpha) = 1\), which shows that \(t_\alpha\) is a section of \(\operatorname{Centr}(G)\). Set \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = X_{2\alpha+\beta}. \] One has at once \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = \alpha(t_\beta) X_\alpha = -X_\alpha, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = \beta(t_\alpha) X_\beta = X_\beta. \] Since \((2\alpha + \beta) + \beta\) and \((2\alpha + \beta) - \beta\) are not roots, one has \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}. \] There exists a scalar \(k \in \mathbb{G}_m(S)\) with \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = k X_{\alpha+\beta}. \] On the other hand, by Exp. XXII, 5.5.2, there exist sections \(A, B, C \in \mathbb{G}_a(S)\) with \[ (1) \qquad p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(A x y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(B x^2 y), \] \[ (2) \qquad p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(C x y). \] In (ii) and (iii), it is therefore a matter of proving that \(A = B = 1\), \(C = 2\), \(k = -1\).

Let us make \(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\) act on formula (2). One finds \[ (3) \qquad p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{-\alpha}(-x) = p_{-\alpha}(-x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(A k x y)\, p_\beta(B x^2 y). \] Transforming (2) in the same way, one obtains \[ (4) \qquad p_{\alpha+\beta}(ky)\, p_{-\alpha}(-x) = p_{-\alpha}(-x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(ky)\, p_\beta(C x y). \] Transforming (1) by \(\operatorname{int}(w_\beta)\), one has \[ (5) \qquad p_{-\beta}(-y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-y)\, p_\alpha(-A x y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(B x^2 y). \]

Let us write \[ w_\beta\, p_\alpha(x)\, w_\beta^{-1} = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x). \] Since \(\alpha + 2\beta\) is not a root, this gives \[ p_\beta(1)\, p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(-1) = p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-1). \] Using (1) on the left-hand side and (5) on the right, \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2)\, p_\beta(-1) = \] \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(-Bx^2)\, p_{-\beta}(-1). \] Since \(p_\beta\) commutes with \(p_{\alpha+\beta}\) and \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}\) on the one hand, and \(p_{-\beta}\) commutes with \(p_\alpha\) and \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}\) on the other, this reads \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(-Bx^2). \] Transforming the right-hand side by (2), \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2) = p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}((AC - B) x^2), \] whence finally \[ A = 1, \qquad C = 2B. \]

Let us now write \[ w_\alpha\, p_\beta(y)\, w_\alpha^{-1} = p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y). \] Since \(3\alpha + \beta\) is not a root, this gives \[ p_\alpha(1)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(-1) = p_{-\alpha}(1)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1). \] Using (1) on the left-hand side and (3) on the right, one obtains \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-Ay)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(By) = p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Aky)\, p_\beta(By). \] Since \(p_{\alpha+\beta}\), \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}\), and \(p_\beta\) commute, this gives at once \[ B = 1, \qquad -A = Ak, \] whence finally \[ A = 1, \qquad B = 1, \qquad C = 2, \qquad k = -1. \]

We have thus proved (ii) and (iii). Let us prove (i): \[ w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha = w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha^{-1}\, t_\alpha = w_{2\alpha+\beta}\, t_\alpha, \] \[ w_\beta w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha w_\beta = w_\beta w_{2\alpha+\beta} w_\beta^{-1} \cdot s_\beta(t_\alpha) \cdot t_\beta = w_{2\alpha+\beta}\, t_\alpha t_\beta, \] \[ w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha = w_\alpha w_{2\alpha+\beta} w_\alpha^{-1} \cdot s_\alpha(t_\alpha t_\beta) \cdot t_\alpha = w_\beta \cdot t_\alpha \cdot t_\beta t_\alpha \cdot t_\alpha = w_\beta^{-1}\, t_\alpha, \] whence \[ (w_\beta w_\alpha)^4 = t_\alpha, \] and \[ (w_\alpha w_\beta)^4 = s_\beta(t_\alpha) = t_\alpha, \] which completes the proof.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.3.7

Condition (v) of 2.3 translates here in the following manner, on setting \(v_{\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\beta) v_\alpha\) and \(v_{2\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha) v_\beta\): \[ (A) \begin{cases} \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha h_\beta h_\alpha)\, v_\beta = v_\beta, \\ \operatorname{int}(h_\beta h_\alpha h_\beta)\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha, \end{cases} \qquad (B) \begin{cases} v_\beta\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_\beta\, v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}^2, \\ v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_{\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{\alpha+\beta} = v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}. \end{cases} \]
3.4. Groups of type \(G_2\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(G_2\); let us write \(R_0 = \{\alpha, \beta\}\), \(R^+ = \{\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + 2\beta\}\).

  1. (i)

    One has \[ t_{\alpha\beta} = (w_\alpha w_\beta)^6 = e = (w_\beta w_\alpha)^6 = t_{\beta\alpha}. \]

  2. (ii)

    If one sets \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = -X_{3\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{3\alpha+\beta} = X_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \] one has: \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = -X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{3\alpha+\beta} = X_\beta, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{3\alpha+2\beta} = X_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = -X_\alpha, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{3\alpha+2\beta} = -X_{3\alpha+\beta}. \]

  3. (iii)

    If one sets \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{\alpha+\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\beta)\, p_\alpha(x), \] \[ p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{2\alpha+\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha w_\beta)\, p_\alpha(x), \] \[ p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{3\alpha+\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\, p_\beta(-x), \] \[ p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x) = \exp(x X_{3\alpha+2\beta}) = \operatorname{int}(w_\beta w_\alpha)\, p_\beta(-x), \] one has: \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x^3 y^2), \] \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(2xy)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(3x^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(3xy^2), \] \[ p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(3xy), \] \[ p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\beta(x) = p_\beta(x)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-xy), \] \[ p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(3xy). \]

We have \((\beta^*, \alpha) = -1\), \((\alpha^*, \beta) = -3\), whence \(\beta(t_\alpha) = \alpha(t_\beta) = -1\). Let us define \(X_{\alpha+\beta}\), \(X_{2\alpha+\beta}\), \(X_{3\alpha+\beta}\) and \(X_{3\alpha+2\beta}\) as in (ii). We have at once \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = \alpha(t_\beta) X_\alpha = -X_\alpha, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = \alpha(t_\alpha)\, \beta(t_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = -X_{\alpha+\beta}, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{3\alpha+\beta} = -\beta(t_\alpha) X_\beta = X_\beta, \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{3\alpha+2\beta} = \alpha(t_\beta)^3\, \beta(t_\beta) X_{3\alpha+\beta} = -X_{3\alpha+\beta}. \] Finally, since \((3\alpha + 2\beta) \pm \alpha\) and \((2\alpha + \beta) \pm \beta\) are not roots, we have: \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{3\alpha+2\beta} = X_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \] which completes the proof of (ii).

By virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.5.2, there exist scalars \[ A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, J \in \mathbb{G}_a(S), \] such that \[ (1)\; p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Axy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Cx^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Dx^3 y^2). \] \[ (2)\; p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Exy)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Fx^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Gxy^2). \] \[ (3)\; p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Hxy). \] \[ (4)\; p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\beta(x) = p_\beta(x)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Jxy). \]

Let us make \(\operatorname{int}(w_\beta)\) act on (1), (3) and (4): \[ (5)\; p_{-\beta}(-y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = \] \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-y)\, p_\alpha(-Axy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Cx^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-Dx^3 y^2). \] \[ (6)\; p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x) = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Hxy). \] \[ (7)\; p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(y)\, p_{-\beta}(-x) = p_{-\beta}(-x)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-Jxy). \] Making \(\operatorname{int}(w_\alpha)\) act in the same way on (1), we find \[ (8)\; p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{-\alpha}(-x) = \] \[ p_{-\alpha}(-x)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Axy)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-Bx^2 y)\, p_\beta(Cx^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Dx^3 y^2). \]

Let us write \[ w_\beta\, p_\alpha(x)\, w_\beta^{-1} = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x), \] that is, \(\alpha + 2\beta\) not being a root: \[ p_\beta(1)\, p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(-1) = p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-1). \] Transforming the left-hand side by (1), then (4) \[ p_\beta(1)\, p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(-1) \] \[ = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Cx^3)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Dx^3)\, p_\beta(-1) \] \[ = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2)\, p_\beta(-1)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Cx^3)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}((D - CJ) x^3) \] \[ = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Bx^2)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Cx^3)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}((D - CJ) x^3). \] Let us transform the right-hand side by (5), then (7): \[ (11)\; p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-1) \] \[ = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(-Bx^2)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-Cx^3)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-Dx^3)\, p_{-\beta}(-1) \] \[ = p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(-Bx^2)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-Cx^3)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}((CJ - D) x^3). \] Using now (2), this right-hand side becomes \[ (12)\; p_\alpha(Ax)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}((AE - B) x^2)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}((A^2 F + CJ - D) x^3)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}((AG - C) x^3). \] Identifying the results obtained, we get: \[ A = 1, \qquad E = 2B, \qquad C + D = F + CJ, \qquad F = G. \]

Let us now write \[ w_\alpha\, p_\beta(y)\, w_\alpha^{-1} = p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y), \] that is, \(4\alpha + \beta\) not being a root: \[ p_\alpha(1)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(-1) = p_{-\alpha}(1)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1). \] Transforming the left-hand side by (1): \[ p_\alpha(1)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(-1) = p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-Ay)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(By)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-Cy)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-Dy^2). \] Let us transform the right-hand side successively by (8), (6) and (4): \[ p_{-\alpha}(1)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1) \] \[ = p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Ay)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-By)\, p_\beta(Cy)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Dy^2) \] \[ = p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-By)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Ay)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-ABHy^2)\, p_\beta(Cy)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(Dy^2) \] \[ = p_\beta(Cy)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-By)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Ay)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}((D - CJ - ABH) y^2) \] \[ = p_\beta(Cy)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(-By)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(Ay)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}((D - CJ - ABH) y^2). \] Identifying \[ C = 1, \qquad A = B, \qquad D - CJ - ABH = -D. \] Taking into account the results already obtained: \[ A = B = C = 1, \qquad E = 2, \qquad F = G, \] \[ D + 1 = F + J, \qquad 2D = H + J. \]

Let us write \[ w_\beta\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x)\, w_\beta^{-1} = p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x), \] that is \[ p_\beta(1)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_\beta(-1) = p_{-\beta}(1)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x)\, p_{-\beta}(-1). \] Transforming the left-hand side by (4), the right-hand side by (7), we obtain: \[ p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-Jx) = p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(-Jx), \] that is \(J = -1\).

Let us finally write \[ w_\alpha\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, w_\alpha^{-1} = p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y), \] that is \[ p_\alpha(1)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(-1) = p_{-\alpha}(1)\, p_\alpha(-1)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(1)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1). \] Transforming the left-hand side by (2), the right-hand side by (3), we obtain: \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(-Ey)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Fy)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-Gy^2) = \] \[ p_{-\alpha}(1)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Hy)\, p_{-\alpha}(-1). \] It is immediate to see that if one commutes \(p_{-\alpha}(-1)\) past \(p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Hy)\), then past \(p_{2\alpha+\beta}(y)\), one introduces no new terms in \(p_{3\alpha+\beta}\) into the right-hand side. The latter is therefore written, denoting by empty parentheses the quantities whose exact value is of no importance to us: \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(\;)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(\;)\, p_\beta(\;)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(Hy)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(\;). \] Comparing with the left-hand side, we have at once \(F = H\), whence by the earlier results \(2D = D + 1\), that is \(D = 1\), and finally \(F = G = H = 2D - J = 3\), which completes the determination of the coefficients \(A, \ldots, J\) and the proof of (iii).

Let us finally prove (i) in the usual manner: \[ w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha = w_\alpha w_\beta w_\alpha^{-1}\, t_\alpha = w_{3\alpha+\beta}^{-1} \cdot t_\alpha, \] \[ w_\beta(w_\alpha w_\beta)^2 = w_\beta w_{3\alpha+\beta}^{-1} w_\beta^{-1} \cdot s_\beta(t_\alpha) \cdot t_\beta = w_{3\alpha+2\beta}^{-1} \cdot t_\alpha t_\beta \cdot t_\beta = w_{3\alpha+2\beta}^{-1} \cdot t_\alpha, \] \[ w_\alpha(w_\beta w_\alpha)^3 = w_\alpha w_{3\alpha+2\beta}^{-1} w_\alpha^{-1} = w_{3\alpha+2\beta}^{-1}, \] \[ w_\beta(w_\alpha w_\beta)^4 = w_\beta w_{3\alpha+2\beta}^{-1} w_\beta^{-1} \cdot t_\beta = w_{3\alpha+\beta} \cdot t_\beta, \] \[ w_\alpha(w_\beta w_\alpha)^5 = w_\alpha w_{3\alpha+\beta} w_\alpha^{-1} \cdot s_\alpha(t_\beta) \cdot t_\alpha = w_\beta \cdot t_\beta t_\alpha \cdot t_\alpha = w_\beta^{-1}. \] Whence \[ (w_\alpha w_\beta)^6 = (w_\beta w_\alpha)^6 = e. \]
