blocks.html:
Remark 3.4.10

Condition (v) of 2.4 is made up of \[ (A) \begin{cases} \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha h_\beta h_\alpha h_\beta h_\alpha)\, v_\beta = v_\beta, \\ \operatorname{int}(h_\beta h_\alpha h_\beta h_\alpha h_\beta)\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha, \end{cases} \] and, setting \[ v_{\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\beta) v_\alpha, \qquad v_{2\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha h_\beta) v_\alpha, \] \[ v_{3\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha) v_\beta^{-1}, \qquad v_{3\alpha+2\beta} = \operatorname{int}(h_\beta h_\alpha) v_\beta^{-1}, \] of the commutation relations: \[ (B) \begin{cases} v_\beta\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_\beta\, v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \\ v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}^2\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}^3\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}^3, \\ v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}^3, \\ v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{3\alpha+2\beta}\, v_\alpha = v_\alpha\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \end{cases} \] \[ (B) \begin{cases} v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_{\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}^{-1}, \\ v_{3\alpha+2\beta}\, v_\beta = v_\beta\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \\ v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{\alpha+\beta} = v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}^3, \end{cases} \] \[ (B) \begin{cases} v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_{\alpha+\beta} = v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{3\alpha+2\beta}\, v_{\alpha+\beta} = v_{\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \\ v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta} = v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+\beta}, \\ v_{3\alpha+2\beta}\, v_{2\alpha+\beta} = v_{2\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \\ v_{3\alpha+2\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+\beta} = v_{3\alpha+\beta}\, v_{3\alpha+2\beta}. \end{cases} \]
3.5. Explicit form of the theorem on generators and relations

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.5.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(T\) its maximal torus, \(R_0\) its system of simple roots, \(u_\alpha \in U_\alpha(S)^*\) and \(w_\alpha \in \operatorname{Norm}_G(T)(S)\) the elements defined by the pinning \((\alpha \in R_0)\). Let \[ f_T : T \longrightarrow H, \qquad f_\alpha : U_\alpha \longrightarrow H, \quad \alpha \in R_0 \] be group morphisms, \(H\) being an \(S\)-sheaf of groups for (fppf); let \(h_\alpha \in H(S)\), \((\alpha \in R_0)\) be sections of \(H\), and set \(v_\alpha = f_\alpha(u_\alpha)\), \(\alpha \in R_0\). For there to exist a group morphism \[ f : G \longrightarrow H \] extending \(f_T\), \(f_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) and satisfying \(f(w_\alpha) = h_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) (and then necessarily unique), it is necessary and sufficient that the following conditions be satisfied:

  1. (i)

    For every \(S' \to S\), every \(\alpha \in R_0\), every \(t \in T(S')\) and every \(x \in U_\alpha(S')\), we have \[ (1) \qquad \operatorname{int}(f_T(t))\, f_\alpha(x) = f_\alpha(\operatorname{int}(t) x) = f_\alpha(x^{\alpha(t)}). \]

  2. (ii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\), every \(S' \to S\) and every \(t \in T(S')\), we have \[ (2) \qquad \operatorname{int}(h_\alpha)\, f_T(t) = f_T(s_\alpha(t)) = f_T(t \cdot \alpha^*(\alpha(t)^{-1})). \]

  3. (iii)

    For every \(\alpha \in R_0\), we have \[ (3_1) \qquad h_\alpha^2 = f_T(\alpha^*(-1)), \] \[ (4) \qquad (h_\alpha\, v_\alpha)^3 = e. \]

  4. (iv)

    For every pair \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), \(\alpha \neq \beta\), such that \((\alpha^*, \beta) = 0\) (resp. \((\alpha^*, \beta) = (\beta^*, \alpha) = -1\), resp. \((\alpha^*, \beta) = -2\), resp. \((\alpha^*, \beta) = -3\)), we have:

    (a) the relation \[ (3_2) \begin{cases} (h_\alpha h_\beta)^2 = f_T(\alpha^*(-1)\, \beta^*(-1)) & \text{if } (\alpha^*, \beta) = 0\ ; \\ (h_\alpha h_\beta)^3 = e, & \text{if } (\alpha^*, \beta) = -1\ ; \\ (h_\alpha h_\beta)^4 = f_T(\alpha^*(-1)), & \text{if } (\alpha^*, \beta) = -2\ ; \\ (h_\alpha h_\beta)^6 = e, & \text{if } (\alpha^*, \beta) = -3. \end{cases} \]

    (b) The relations (A) of 3.1.3 (resp. 3.2.8, resp. 3.3.7, resp. 3.4.10);

    (c) The (resp. the three, resp. the six, resp. the fifteen) relation(s) (B) of 3.1.3 (resp. 3.2.8, resp. 3.3.7, resp. 3.4.10).

This follows at once from 2.3, 2.6 and from the computations made in each particular case.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.5.2

The preceding results may be presented in a slightly different manner: one gives oneself morphisms, for \(\alpha \in R_0\), \[ a_\alpha : T \cdot U_\alpha \longrightarrow H, \qquad b_\alpha : \operatorname{Norm}_{Z_\alpha}(T) \longrightarrow H\ ; \] the conditions to be checked are the following: (1) all the \(a_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) and all the \(b_\alpha\) \((\alpha \in R_0)\) have the same restriction to \(T\); (2) for every \(\alpha \in R_0\), set \[ h_\alpha = b_\alpha(w_\alpha), \qquad v_\alpha = a_\alpha(u_\alpha)\ ; \] then one has, for every \(\alpha \in R_0\), the relation \[ (h_\alpha\, v_\alpha)^3 = e, \] and the conditions of (iv) above are satisfied.

Various applications of this theorem will be given in the next exposé. Let us point out one of them here: theorem 3.5.1 gives a description of \(G\) by generators and relations in the category of \(S\)-sheaves for (fppf); in other words, let us consider, for each \(S' \to S\), the group \(H(S')\) generated by \(T(S')\), \(U_\alpha(S')\), \(\alpha \in R\), and \(w_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R\), subject to the relations analogous to \((1) \ldots (3_2)\), (A), (B); then \(G\) is none other than the sheaf associated with the presheaf \(S' \mapsto H(S')\).

In particular, if \(S'\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\), we have \(G(S') = H(S')\) (an immediate consequence of the Nullstellensatz in the form: "a sieve of an algebraically closed field which is covering for (fppf) is trivial"), so that 3.5.1 gives at once an explicit description by generators and relations of the "abstract" group \(G(k)\).

pages.title: 4. Uniqueness of pinned groups: fundamental theorem

blocks.html: 4. Uniqueness of pinned groups: fundamental theorem

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1

Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme. The functor \(\mathcal{R}\) of 1.6 is fully faithful: let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two pinned \(S\)-groups, \(q\) an integer \(> 0\) such that \(x \mapsto x^q\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathbb{G}_{a, S}\), and \(h : \mathcal{R}(G') \to \mathcal{R}(G)\) a \(q\)-morphism of pinned root data. There exists a unique morphism of pinned groups \[ f : G \longrightarrow G' \] such that \(\mathcal{R}(f) = h\).

Uniqueness is proved in 1.9. It suffices to prove existence. By hypothesis, we have a bijection \(u : R \xrightarrow{\sim} R'\) and a map \(q : R \to q^{\mathbb{N}}\) such that \[ h(u(\alpha)) = q(\alpha) \alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad {}^t h(\alpha^*) = q(\alpha) u(\alpha)^* \] for every \(\alpha \in R\). In particular, the semi-simple ranks of \(G\) and \(G'\) coincide.

Suppose \(\operatorname{rgss}(G) = \operatorname{rgss}(G') = 0\). Then \(G\) and \(G'\) are tori: we have \(G = T = D_S(M)\), \(G' = T' = D_S(M')\) and \(h\) is simply a morphism of ordinary groups \(h : M' \to M\). We then take \(f = D_S(h)\).

Suppose \(\operatorname{rgss}(G) = \operatorname{rgss}(G') = 1\). Let us then consider \[ f_T = D_S(h) : T \longrightarrow T'. \] By hypothesis we have a commutative diagram, where \(\alpha' = u(\alpha)\): \[ \begin{array}{ccccc} \mathbb{G}_{m,S} & \xrightarrow{\alpha^*} & T & \xrightarrow{\alpha} & \mathbb{G}_{m,S} \\ {}^{q(\alpha)}\!\!\downarrow & & \downarrow^{f_T} & & \downarrow^{q(\alpha)} \\ \mathbb{G}_{m,S} & \xrightarrow{\alpha'^*} & T' & \xrightarrow{\alpha'} & \mathbb{G}_{m,S} \end{array} \] One then applies Exp. XX, 4.1.

Suppose \(\operatorname{rgss}(G) = \operatorname{rgss}(G') = 2\). Then, by Exp. XXI, 7.5.3, one knows all the possibilities for \(h : \mathcal{R}(G') \to \mathcal{R}(G)\). Let us study them one after the other, checking in each case the conditions of 2.5.
Let us write \(R_0 = \{\alpha, \beta\}\), \(R'_0 = \{\alpha', \beta'\}\) in such a way that \(u(\alpha) = \alpha'\), \(u(\beta) = \beta'\).

\(G\) and \(G'\) of type \(A_1 + A_1\). We then have \[ h(\alpha') = q\alpha, \qquad h(\beta') = q_1 \beta. \] Let us show that the conditions of 2.5 are satisfied. By 3.1.2 (ii) (resp. (iii)), (ii) (resp. (iii)) is trivial. Let us prove (i). We have \[ D_S(h) t_{\alpha\beta} = D_S(h)(t_\alpha t_\beta) = {}^t h(\alpha^*)(-1) \cdot {}^t h(\beta^*)(-1) \] \[ = \alpha'^*(-1)^q\, \beta'^*(-1)^q = \alpha'^*(-1)\, \beta'^*(-1) = t'_{\alpha' \beta'}. \]

\(G\) and \(G'\) of type \(A_2\). We then have \[ h(\alpha') = q\alpha, \qquad h(\beta') = q\beta. \] Set \(X_{\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha\) and \(X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_{\beta'}) X_{\alpha'}\). Let us check the conditions of 2.5. For (i), one argues as above, with the help of 3.2.1 (i); for (ii), it is immediate by 3.2.1 (ii); it remains to check (iii). We have to check that \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(z) \longmapsto p'_{\alpha'}(x^q)\, p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(z^q) \] is a group morphism. The only non-trivial commutation relation is that of 3.2.1 (iii), which is written \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy), \] \[ p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'}(x^q) = p'_{\alpha'}(x^q)\, p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(x^q y^q). \]

One argues in the same way for \(G\) and \(G'\) of type \(B_2\) (resp. \(G_2\)), when the root exponents are equal, with the help of 3.3.1 (resp. 3.4.1); it therefore remains, in order to complete the case of groups of rank 2, to treat the two exceptional cases of Exp. XXI, 7.5.3.

\(G\) and \(G'\) are of type \(B_2\), \(S\) is of characteristic 2, and one has \(q(\alpha) = 2q\), \(q(\beta) = q\). The positive roots are \(\{\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta\}\) and \(\{\alpha', \beta', \alpha' + \beta', \alpha' + 2\beta'\}\) (note that the "short" roots are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta'\)). We have \[ h(\alpha') = 2q\alpha, \quad h(\beta') = q\beta, \quad h(\alpha' + \beta') = q(2\alpha + \beta), \quad h(\alpha' + 2\beta') = 2q(\alpha + \beta), \] which gives \[ u(\alpha + \beta) = \alpha' + 2\beta', \qquad q(\alpha + \beta) = 2q, \] \[ u(2\alpha + \beta) = \alpha' + \beta', \qquad q(2\alpha + \beta) = q. \] Set \[ X_{\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha, \qquad X_{2\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta, \] \[ X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{\beta'}, \qquad X'_{\alpha'+2\beta'} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'}. \] Let us now check the conditions of 2.5.
(i) Since \(S\) is of characteristic 2, one has \(-1 = 1\) on \(S\), hence \(t_{\alpha\beta} = t_\alpha = \alpha^*(-1) = e = \beta'^*(-1) = t'_{\beta'} = t'_{\alpha'\beta'}\) (cf. 3.3.1 (i)).

(ii) By construction one has \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{\beta'} = X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = X'_{u(2\alpha+\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'} = X'_{\alpha'+2\beta'} = X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)}. \] By 3.3.1 (ii) and the fact that \(-1 = 1\) on \(S\), one has on both sides \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = X_{\alpha+\beta}, \quad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)} = X'_{\alpha'+2\beta'} = X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_\beta, \quad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{u(2\alpha+\beta)} = X'_{\beta'} = X'_{u(\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{\alpha+\beta} = X_\alpha, \quad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)} = X'_{\alpha'} = X'_{u(\alpha)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \quad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{u(2\alpha+\beta)} = X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = X'_{u(2\alpha+\beta)}. \]

(iii) By 3.3.1 (iii), one sees that the only non-trivial commutation relation in \(U\) (resp. \(U'\)) is \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y), \] resp. \[ p'_{\alpha'}(y')\, p'_{\beta'}(x') = p'_{\beta'}(x')\, p'_{\alpha'}(y')\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(x' y')\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}(x'^2 y'). \] We must check that the morphism \[ p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(z)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(t) \longmapsto p'_{\alpha'}(x^{2q})\, p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}(z^{2q})\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(t^q) \] is a group morphism; one sees at once that this amounts to seeing that \[ p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'}(x^{2q}) = p'_{\alpha'}(x^{2q})\, p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}((xy)^{2q})\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}((x^2 y)^q), \] which is none other than the second relation above (on setting \(y' = x^{2q}\), \(x' = y^q\)).

\(G\) and \(G'\) are of type \(G_2\), \(S\) is of characteristic 3, and one has \[ q(\alpha) = 3q, \qquad q(\beta) = q. \] The positive roots are \(\{\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta, 2\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + \beta, 3\alpha + 2\beta\}\) on the one hand, and \(\{\alpha', \beta', \alpha' + \beta', \alpha' + 2\beta', \alpha' + 3\beta', 2\alpha' + 3\beta'\}\) on the other (as in the preceding case, the short roots are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta'\)). We have \[ h(\alpha') = 3q\alpha, \quad h(\beta') = q\beta, \quad h(\alpha' + \beta') = q(3\alpha + \beta), \] \[ h(\alpha' + 2\beta') = q(3\alpha + 2\beta), \quad h(\alpha' + 3\beta') = 3q(\alpha + \beta), \] \[ h(2\alpha' + 3\beta') = 3q(2\alpha + \beta), \] which gives \[ u(\alpha + \beta) = \alpha' + 3\beta', \quad q(\alpha + \beta) = 3q, \] \[ u(2\alpha + \beta) = 2\alpha' + 3\beta', \quad q(2\alpha + \beta) = 3q, \] \[ u(3\alpha + \beta) = \alpha' + \beta', \quad q(3\alpha + \beta) = q, \] \[ u(3\alpha + 2\beta) = \alpha' + 2\beta', \quad q(3\alpha + 2\beta) = q. \] Set \[ X_{\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha, \qquad X_{2\alpha+\beta} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta}, \] \[ X_{3\alpha+\beta} = -\operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta, \qquad X_{3\alpha+2\beta} = \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{3\alpha+\beta}\ ; \] \[ X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = -\operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{\beta'}, \qquad X'_{\alpha'+2\beta'} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'+\beta'}, \] \[ X'_{\alpha'+3\beta'} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'}, \qquad X'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}. \] Let us now check the conditions of 2.5.
(i) One has \(t_{\alpha\beta} = e\) and \(t'_{\alpha'\beta'} = e\) by 3.4.1 (i).

(ii) By construction one has \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_\alpha = X_{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'} = X'_{\alpha'+3\beta'} = X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_\beta = -X_{3\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{\beta'} = -X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = -X'_{u(3\alpha+\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{3\alpha+\beta} = X_{3\alpha+2\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{u(3\alpha+\beta)} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = X'_{\alpha'+2\beta'} = X'_{u(3\alpha+2\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{\alpha+\beta} = X_{2\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{\alpha'+3\beta'} = X'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'} = X'_{u(2\alpha+\beta)}. \]

By 3.4.1 (ii), one has on both sides: \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha) X_{2\alpha+\beta} = -X_{\alpha+\beta}, \quad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{u(2\alpha+\beta)} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\alpha'}) X'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'} = -X'_{\alpha'+3\beta'} = -X'_{u(\alpha+\beta)}\ ; \] \[ \cdots \] \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\beta) X_{3\alpha+2\beta} = -X_{3\alpha+\beta}, \quad \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{u(3\alpha+2\beta)} = \operatorname{Ad}(w'_{\beta'}) X'_{\alpha'+2\beta'} = -X'_{\alpha'+\beta'} = -X'_{u(3\alpha+\beta)}. \] (The dots stand for 4 verifications of the same kind).

(iii) The only non-trivial commutation relations in \(U\) and \(U'\) are, by 3.4.1 (iii) (and taking into account that \(3 = 0\) on \(S\)): \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(x^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(x^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(x^3 y^2), \] \[ p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(-xy), \] \[ p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_\beta(x) = p_\beta(x)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(-xy)\ ; \] \[ p'_{\alpha'}(y')\, p'_{\beta'}(x') = \] \[ p'_{\beta'}(x')\, p'_{\alpha'}(y')\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(-x'y')\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}(-x'^2 y')\, p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}(-x'^3 y')\, p'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'}(-x'^3 y'^2), \] \[ p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(y')\, p'_{\beta'}(x') = p'_{\beta'}(x')\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(y')\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}(x'y'), \] \[ p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}(y')\, p'_{\alpha'}(x') = p'_{\alpha'}(x')\, p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}(y')\, p'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'}(x'y'). \] We have to check that the morphism \(\varphi\) from \(U\) into \(U'\) defined by \[ \varphi\!\left(p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(t)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(u)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(v)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(w)\right) \] \[ = p'_{\alpha'}(x^{3q})\, p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}(t^{3q})\, p'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'}(u^{3q})\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(v^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}(w^q) \] is a group morphism. Now one checks immediately that the last three commutation relations may also be written \[ p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'}(x^{3q}) = \] \[ p'_{\alpha'}(x^{3q})\, p'_{\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}((xy)^{3q})\, p'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'}((x^2 y)^{3q})\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}((x^3 y)^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}((x^3 y^2)^q), \] \[ p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}(y^{3q})\, p'_{\alpha'}(x^{3q}) = p'_{\alpha'}(x^{3q})\, p'_{\alpha'+3\beta'}(y^{3q})\, p'_{2\alpha'+3\beta'}(-(xy)^{3q}), \] \[ p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\beta'}(x^q) = p'_{\beta'}(x^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+\beta'}(y^q)\, p'_{\alpha'+2\beta'}(-(xy)^q)\ ; \] which shows that \(\varphi\) is indeed a group morphism and completes the proof of 4.1.7.

Case where \(G\) and \(G'\) are of semi-simple rank \(\geqslant 2\). For each root \(\alpha \in R_0\), let \(\alpha' = u(\alpha) \in R'_0 = u(R_0)\). For each \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\), consider the pinned groups of semi-simple rank \(\leqslant 2\), \(Z_{\alpha\beta}\) and \(Z'_{\alpha'\beta'}\). The group morphism \(M' \to M\) underlying \(h\) defines a \(q\)-morphism of root data \[ h_{\alpha\beta} : \mathcal{R}(Z_{\alpha\beta}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}(Z'_{\alpha'\beta'}). \] By the preceding results, there therefore exists a morphism of pinned groups \[ f_{\alpha\beta} : Z_{\alpha\beta} \longrightarrow Z'_{\alpha'\beta'} \] such that \(\mathcal{R}(f_{\alpha\beta}) = h_{\alpha\beta}\). Let us prove that the \(f_{\alpha\beta}\) satisfy the gluing condition of 2.5; indeed \(f_{\alpha\beta}|_{Z_\alpha}\) and \(f_{\alpha\alpha}\) are two morphisms of pinned groups \[ Z_\alpha \longrightarrow Z'_{\alpha'} \] corresponding to the same morphism of pinned root data, and hence coincide by the uniqueness result already proved. By 2.5 there therefore exists a group morphism \[ f : G \longrightarrow G' \] extending the \(f_{\alpha\beta}\). This is obviously a morphism of pinned groups such that \(\mathcal{R}(f) = h\), which completes the proof of Theorem 4.1.
5. Corollaries of the fundamental theorem
The most important one is:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.1

Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two pinned \(S\)-groups, \(h\) an isomorphism of pinned root data \[ h : \mathcal{R}(G') \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathcal{R}(G). \] There exists a unique isomorphism of pinned \(S\)-groups \[ f : G \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} G' \] such that \(\mathcal{R}(f) = h\).

Note that 5.1 also follows from 3.5.1 (the relations of 3.5.1 can be written using only the datum \(\mathcal{R}(G)\)); note also that 5.1 follows from the most elementary part of the proof of 4.1 (there is no need to consider the "exceptional isogenies" of 4.1.7 and 4.1.8).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2 ("Uniqueness theorem")

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two splittable \(S\)-groups (Exp. XXII, 1.13). If \(G\) and \(G'\) are of the same type (Exp. XXII, 2.6), they are isomorphic.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) and \(G'\) two splittable \(S\)-groups. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic.

  2. (ii)

    \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic locally for the (fpqc) topology.

  3. (iii)

    There exists an \(s \in S\) such that the \(s\)-groups \(G_s\) and \(G'_s\) are of the same type.

Indeed, one obviously has (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii). On the other hand, (iii) implies that \(\mathcal{R}(G) = \mathcal{R}(G_s) = \mathcal{R}(G'_s) = \mathcal{R}(G')\), hence that \(G\) and \(G'\) satisfy the condition of 5.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.4 ("uniqueness of Chevalley schemes")

Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two reductive \(\mathbb{Z}\)-groups possessing trivial maximal tori. * The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic.

  2. (ii)

    There exists \(s \in \operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})\) such that \(G_s\) and \(G'_s\) are of the same type.

  3. (iii)

    \(G_{\mathbb{C}}\) and \(G'_{\mathbb{C}}\) are of the same type.

Indeed \(G\) and \(G'\) are splittable by Exp. XXII, 2.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5 ("Existence of outer automorphisms")

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a pinned \(S\)-group, \(h\) an automorphism of the pinned root datum \(\mathcal{R}(G)\). There exists a unique automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) respecting its pinning and such that \(\mathcal{R}(u) = h\).
Let us make the preceding corollary explicit:

blocks.label: 5.5.bis
blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5.bis

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a split reductive \(S\)-group, \(R^+\) a system of positive roots of \(G\). For each simple root \(\alpha\), choose an isomorphism of vector groups \(p_\alpha : \mathbb{G}_{a, S} \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} U_\alpha\). Let \(h\) be an automorphism of \(M\) permuting the positive roots and the corresponding coroots: if \(\alpha \in R^+\), \(h(\alpha) \in R^+\) and \(h^\vee(\alpha^*) = h(\alpha)^*\). There exists a unique automorphism \(u\) of \(G\) inducing \(D_S(h)\) on \(T\) and such that \(u \circ p_\alpha = p_{h(\alpha)}\) for every simple root \(\alpha\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6

Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be two reductive \(S\)-groups. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic locally for (fpqc).

  2. (i bis)

    \(G\) and \(G'\) are isomorphic locally for the étale topology.

  3. (ii)

    For every \(s \in S\), \(G_s\) and \(G'_s\) are isomorphic.

  4. (iii)

    The functions \(s \mapsto \text{type of } G_s\) and \(s \mapsto \text{type of } G'_s\) are equal.

Indeed (i bis) \(\Rightarrow\) (i) trivially, (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) by the principle of finite extension, (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) trivially; it remains to prove (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i bis). Now one may assume \(G\) and \(G'\) splittable (Exp. XXII, 2.3), in which case the assertion follows from 5.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(G'\) an affine, smooth \(S\)-group with connected fibres. Let \(s \in S\) be such that \(G_s\) and \(G'_s\) are isomorphic; there exists an \(S' \to S\) étale and covering \(s\) such that \(G_{S'}\) and \(G'_{S'}\) are isomorphic.
Indeed, by Exp. XIX 2.3 and Exp. XXII 2.1, one may assume \(G\) and \(G'\) reductive and splittable, and we are reduced to 5.3.
In the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, one deduces from 5.6 and 5.7:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.8

Let \(k\) be a field and \(G\) and \(G'\) two reductive \(k\)-groups. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    \(G\) and \(G'\) are of the same type.

  2. (ii)

    \(G \otimes_k \bar{k}\) and \(G' \otimes_k \bar{k}\) are isomorphic.

  3. (iii)

    There exists a finite separable extension \(K\) of \(k\) such that \(G \otimes_k K\) and \(G' \otimes_k K\) are isomorphic.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9

Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme and \(\mathcal{R}\) a root datum. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    There exists a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\).

  2. (ii)

    There exists an \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\).

  3. (iii)

    There exists locally for (fpqc) a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\).

It is obviously a matter of proving (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i). To simplify the proof, let us suppose that there exists a faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism \(S' \to S\) and a reductive \(S'\)-group \(G'\) of type \(\mathcal{R}\). One may assume \(G'\) splittable; let us fix a pinning \(E'\) of \(G'\); write \(\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{R}(G', E')\). The two inverse images of \((G', E')\) on \(S'' = S' \times_S S'\) are pinned groups \((G''_1, E''_1)\), \((G''_2, E''_2)\); one has canonical isomorphisms \(p_i : \mathcal{R}(G''_i, E''_i) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{R}\), whence an isomorphism \[ p = p_2^{-1} \circ p_1 : \mathcal{R}(G''_1, E''_1) \longrightarrow \mathcal{R}(G''_2, E''_2). \] By the uniqueness theorem, there exists a unique isomorphism \[ f : (G''_1, E''_1) \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} (G''_2, E''_2) \] such that \(\mathcal{R}(f) = p\). We thus have on \(G'\) a gluing datum; it is a descent datum.

Indeed, one must verify a compatibility condition between the inverse images of \(f\) on \(S'''\), but it suffices to do so on the transforms of these arrows by \(\mathcal{R}\), since the latter is fully faithful. Now \(p\) is indeed a descent datum, by construction, which shows that \(f\) is one as well. Since \(G'\) is affine, this descent datum is effective; since the pinning of \(G'\) is stable under the descent datum, one verifies easily that there exists a pinned \(S\)-group \((G, E)\) which gives \((G', E')\) by base extension and which is therefore of type \(\mathcal{R}\).
N. B. Naturally, in the language of fibred categories, the preceding proof simplifies (and becomes intelligible).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.10

Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme. Let \(\mathcal{R}\) be a pinned root datum such that there exists a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\). Then there exists a pinned \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\), unique up to a unique isomorphism.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.11

Under the preceding conditions, we shall denote by \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathcal{R})\) the unique pinned \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\), by \(T_S(\mathcal{R})\) its canonical maximal torus, by \(B_S(\mathcal{R})\) its canonical Borel group, \(\ldots\)

If one has a morphism \(S' \to S\) (\(S'\) non-empty), one may identify \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_{S'}(\mathcal{R})\) with \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathcal{R}) \times_S S'\), etc... In particular, if \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_{\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})}(\mathcal{R})\) exists (we shall see that this is always the case), it is denoted by \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}(\mathcal{R})\) and one has \[ \operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathcal{R}) = \operatorname{\acute{E}p}(\mathcal{R}) \times_{\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})} S. \] One says that \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}(\mathcal{R})\) is the Chevalley group scheme of type \(\mathcal{R}\).

It thus amounts to the same to say that the \(S\)-group sheaf \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\) or to say that it is locally isomorphic (for the étale or (fpqc) topology) to \(\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathcal{R})\). Likewise, by virtue of the conjugacy theorems, it amounts to the same to say that \((G, T)\) is a reductive \(S\)-group of type \(\mathcal{R}\) equipped with a maximal torus or that it is locally isomorphic to \((\operatorname{\acute{E}p}_S(\mathcal{R}), T_S(\mathcal{R}))\); likewise with Borel groups or Killing couples.

footnotes.html: In fact, one can prove that every \(\mathbb{Z}\)-torus is trivial.

blocks.html: 6. Chevalley systems
The explicit computations of no. 3 have important numerical consequences. Let us first lay down the following definition:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group. By a Chevalley system of \(G\) is meant a family \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R}\) of elements \[ X_\alpha \in \Gamma(S, \mathfrak{g}_\alpha)^* \] satisfying the following condition:

(SC) for every pair \(\alpha, \beta \in R\), one has \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha(X_\alpha))\, X_\beta = \pm X_{s_\alpha(\beta)}. \]
Recall (Exp. XX, 3.1) that \[ w_\alpha(X_\alpha) = \exp(X_\alpha)\, \exp(-X_\alpha^{-1})\, \exp(X_\alpha). \]

Let us note that (SC) implies in particular \(X_{-\alpha} = \pm X_\alpha\) for \(\alpha \in R\), by virtue of the relation (Exp. XX, 2.10) \(\operatorname{Ad}(w_\alpha(X_\alpha))\, X_\alpha = -X_{-\alpha}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2

Every split group possesses a Chevalley system. More precisely, let \((R_0, (X'_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_0})\) be a pinning (1.1) of the split group \((G, T, M, R)\); there exists a Chevalley system \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R}\) of \(G\) such that \(X_\alpha = X'_\alpha\) for \(\alpha \in R_0\).

Let us first show that it suffices to verify condition (SC) for \(\alpha \in R_0\); for every \(\alpha \in R\), there exists a sequence \(\{\alpha_i\} \subset R_0\) with \(\alpha = s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n}(\alpha_{n+1})\), whence, applying condition (SC) for each of the \(\alpha_i\), \[ X_\alpha = \pm \operatorname{Ad}(w_{\alpha_1}(X_{\alpha_1}) \cdots w_{\alpha_n}(X_{\alpha_n}))\, X_{\alpha_{n+1}}. \] By 3.1.1 (iii), one has \[ w_{\alpha_1}(X_{\alpha_1}) \cdots w_{\alpha_n}(X_{\alpha_n})\, w_{\alpha_{n+1}}(X_{\alpha_{n+1}})\, w_{\alpha_n}(X_{\alpha_n})^{-1} \cdots w_{\alpha_1}(X_{\alpha_1})^{-1} = \alpha^*(\pm 1)\, w_\alpha(X_\alpha). \] Now it suffices to note that \(w_{\alpha_i}(X_{\alpha_i})^{-1} = \alpha_i^*(-1) w_{\alpha_i}(X_{\alpha_i})\) and that for every pair of roots \((\beta, \gamma)\), one has \(\beta(\gamma^*(-1)) = (-1)^{(\gamma^*, \beta)} = \pm 1\), which implies that if (SC) is verified for the pairs \((\alpha_i, \gamma)\) \((\gamma \in R)\), it is so for every pair \((\alpha, \beta)\), \((\beta \in R)\).

Let us now construct a system \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R}\) in the following manner. For every \(\alpha \in R\), choose a sequence \(\{\alpha_i\} \subset R_0\) as above and define \(X_\alpha\) by \[ X_\alpha = \operatorname{Ad}(w_{\alpha_i}(X_{\alpha_1}) \cdots w_{\alpha_n}(X_{\alpha_n}))\, X'_{\alpha_{n+1}}. \] In order to verify (SC), it suffices to prove:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.3

Let \((G, T, M, R, R_0, (X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_0})\) be a pinned \(S\)-group; let \(\alpha_i\) \((0 \leqslant i \leqslant n + 1)\) be a sequence of simple roots such that \[ \operatorname{int}(s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n})(\alpha_{n+1}) = \alpha_0. \] Then \[ \operatorname{Ad}(w_{\alpha_1} \cdots w_{\alpha_n})\, X_{\alpha_{n+1}} = \pm X_{\alpha_0}. \]
Arguing as in 2.3.4 with the help of Tits's lemma, we are reduced to verifying Lemma 6.3 in the following two cases:
a) \(G\) is of semi-simple rank at most 2, or b) \(w_{\alpha_1} \cdots w_{\alpha_n}\) is a section of \(T\).
In case a), let us note that 6.3 is a consequence of 6.2 and that 6.2 has been verified in 3.1.2 (resp. 3.2.1, resp. 3.3.1, resp. 3.4.1), (ii).

It remains, then, to prove 6.3 in case b), or, what amounts to the same, that if \(\{\alpha_i\}\) is a sequence of simple roots such that \(s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n} = \mathrm{id}\), then \(t = w_{\alpha_1} \cdots w_{\alpha_n}\) satisfies \(\alpha(t) = \pm 1\) for every root \(\alpha \in R\). By virtue of the structure of the Weyl group (Exp. XXI, 5.1), the word \(s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n}\) of the free group generated by the \(s_\alpha\), \(\alpha \in R_0\), lies in the invariant subgroup generated by the \((s_\alpha s_\beta)^{n_{\alpha\beta}}\), \((\alpha, \beta) \in R_0 \times R_0\). We are thus reduced to the case where \(s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_n}\) is of the form \[ s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_i}\, (s_{\alpha_{i+1}} s_{\alpha_{i+2}})^{n_{\alpha_{i+1} \alpha_{i+2}}}\, s_{\alpha_i} \cdots s_{\alpha_1}. \] Then one has \[ t = s_{\alpha_1} \cdots s_{\alpha_i}\, (t_{\alpha_{i+1} \alpha_{i+2}}), \] and we are reduced to verifying that for every pair of simple roots \((\alpha_1, \alpha_2)\) and every root \(\beta \in R\), one has \(\beta(t_{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}) = \pm 1\), which is trivial, in view of the values of \(t_{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}\) computed in no. 3 (part (i) of 3.1.2, 3.2.1, 3.3.1, 3.4.1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group, \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R}\) a Chevalley system of \(G\). Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be two non-proportional roots; suppose \[ \operatorname{long}(\alpha) \leqslant \operatorname{long}(\beta), \quad \text{i.e.} \quad |(\beta^*, \alpha)| \leqslant |(\alpha^*, \beta)|. \] Let \(p\) and \(q\) be the integers \(\geqslant 0\) such that the set of roots of the form \(\beta + k\alpha\), \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\), is \[ \{\beta - (p-1)\alpha, \ldots, \beta, \ldots, \beta + q\alpha\}. \] (cf. Exp. XXI, 2.3.5; by loc. cit., one therefore has \(-(\alpha^*, \beta) = q - p + 1\)). Then the commutation relation between \(U_\alpha\) and \(U_\beta\) is given by the following table (which exhausts the possible cases, since the length of the preceding root chain is \(p + q - 1 \leqslant 3\)), where for each \(\gamma \in R\) we write \(p_\gamma(x) = \exp(x X_\gamma)\):

\(p\) arbitrary, \(q = 0\) \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y). \]

\(p = 1\), \(q = 1\) \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm xy). \]

\(p = 1\), \(q = 2\) \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(\pm x^2 y). \]

\(p = 1\), \(q = 3\), \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(\pm x^2 y)\, p_{3\alpha+\beta}(\pm x^3 y)\, p_{3\alpha+2\beta}(\pm x^3 y^2). \]

\(p = 2\), \(q = 1\), \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm 2xy). \]

\(p = 2\), \(q = 2\), \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm 2xy)\, p_{2\alpha+\beta}(\pm 3x^2 y)\, p_{\alpha+2\beta}(\pm 3xy^2). \]

\(p = 3\), \(q = 1\), \[ p_\beta(y)\, p_\alpha(x) = p_\alpha(x)\, p_\beta(y)\, p_{\alpha+\beta}(\pm 3xy). \]

Proof. By virtue of Exp. XXI, 3.5.4, there exists a system of simple roots \(R_0\) of \(R\) such that \(\alpha \in R_0\) and such that there exist \(\alpha' \in R_0\) and \(a, b \geqslant 0\) with \(\beta = a\alpha + b\alpha'\). Consider the pinning \((R_0, (X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_0})\) of \(G\). The commutation relation to be verified is a relation between elements of \(U_{\alpha\alpha'}\); we are thus reduced to the explicit computations of no. 3, and one concludes at once by condition (SC).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.5 (Chevalley's rule)

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R}\) a Chevalley system of the split \(S\)-group \(G\). If \(\alpha, \beta, \alpha + \beta \in R\), then \[ [X_\alpha, X_\beta] = \pm p\, X_{\alpha+\beta}, \] where \(p\) is the smallest integer \(> 0\) such that \(\beta - p\alpha\) is not a root.
Indeed, since the assertion is symmetric in \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), one may assume \(\operatorname{long}(\alpha) \leqslant \operatorname{long}(\beta)\), and we are reduced to 6.4.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme such that \(6 \cdot 1_S \neq 0\) and \((G, T, M, R)\) a split \(S\)-group. If \(R'\) is a subset of \(R\) such that \[ \mathfrak{g}_{R'} = \mathfrak{t} \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R'} \mathfrak{g}_\alpha \] is a Lie subalgebra of \(\mathfrak{g}\), then \(R'\) is a closed subset of \(R\) (Exp. XXI, 3.1.4).

It is possible to make precise the exact value of the various \(\pm\) of this section, thanks to the study of the group \(\operatorname{Norm}_G(T)\) and, more precisely, of the "extended Weyl group": \[ W^* = \operatorname{Norm}_{\operatorname{\acute{E}p}(\mathcal{R})}(T(\mathcal{R}))(\mathbb{Z}) \] which is an extension of \(W(\mathcal{R})\) by an abelian group of type \((2, 2, \ldots, 2)\), and which is "responsible for the signs" **.
